newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's largest airports hit by pay dispute strike.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's largest airports hit by pay dispute strike.

text.p: Kenya's two largest airports were hit by a strike over pay on Saturday and international arrivals were being re-routed, airport officials said.

Air traffic controllers at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) in the capital Nairobi and at Moi International Airport in Mombasa, Kenya's second city and the centre of its tourism industry, began a strike at midnight on Friday (2100 GMT), the officials said.
The strike was bound to increase pressure on the government, rocked by an International Monetary Fund decision on Thursday to halt a big aid package to Kenya.
The IMF suspended a $205 million three-year loan citing concerns over corruption and reform of the energy sector.

The strike caused delays to outgoing flights at JKIA and at least four international arrivals, including three from London, were re-routed to Mombasa, according to an airport information official. Other flights were routed to Kilimanjaro airport in northern Tanzania.
Aircraft re-routed to Mombasa would return to Nairobi after refueling, the official said.
"The strike is on here, our problem is of course money. We don't have enough money," said an air traffic control official who declined to be named.

"There is a go-slow at the moment because the air traffic control tower has been on strike since this morning...All the flights are delayed at the moment and we don't know how long we'll have to wait," said a senior air cargo official.
Numerous airport officials denied a strike or go-slow was in progress in an apparent attempt to calm passengers.

"They (airport authorities) told us the flight was delayed due to weather conditions. Half an hour later they told us there were problems in the operational tower," said a passenger, one of scores who waited in departure lounges or queued for international telephones.
Tourism operators said the strike would hurt their business, reducing the flow of valuable customers from the Europe and the U.S.

"We have been here since early this morning waiting for passengers to come from the U.S. This is terrible, if this strike goes on it could kill the tourist industry," said Francis Ombuni of Park East Safaris.
Around 30 tour minivans lined up outside the airport waiting for passengers expected this morning.

Air traffic controllers staged a strike over pay for several days last December causing long delays at Nairobi and Mombasa airports. They argued their starting salary was equivalent to $90 a month but returned to work after talks with the government.
Tourism is Kenya's biggest hard currency earner with 717,000 visitors in 1996.
